title: Mountains and Waters
speaker: Seiu Hannah Sullivan
summary: Seiu Hannah Sullivan takes up Dogen's Mountains and Waters Sutra from the Shobogenzo, dedicating it to the sangha's wilderness program and its hikers. Seiu reads the opening verses, including "the green mountains are always walking" and the stone woman who gives birth at night, beside the Su Tung Po poem said to have inspired the fascicle. Wendy Johnson chanting the sutra on the walk from Tassajara to Green Gulch, Qingyuan Weixin's mountains-as-mountains passage, and a short turn to water and "blue mind" fill out the middle. Seiu closes with Gary Snyder's poem "Atomic Dawn," in which a young Snyder on Mount St. Helens in August 1945 reads of Hiroshima and vows to fight against atomic destruction.

sentences.text: *Unsurpassed, penetrating and perfect dharma is rarely met with even in a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.*
Good evening.
Thank you for the glasses.
The last Dharma talk I gave, I picked up my iPad to give the talk and the pad was reloading, so I had to give it by heart.
This time I printed, but I forgot the glasses.
What are you going to do?

I wanted to dedicate this evening's talk on Dogen and the Mountains and Rivers Sutra, or Mountains and Waters Sutra, as I see it called intermittently, to our wilderness program and to all of the hikers who have so lovingly chanted this sutra at various times during their backpacking trips.
I also dedicate it to everyone who's spending time outside because it's so beautiful, and to those of us who, for reasons known best unto ourselves, are currently walking in our imagination.
And thank you all for coming in out of the outdoors.
I chose this fascicle we know as the Mountains and Waters Sutra.
It appears in this Treasury of the True Dharma, the Shogo Genzo, as translated by Kaz Tanahashi.
It also appears in this smaller book, Moon in a Dewdrop, which for the student is great because it's all the same stuff, but it's organized a little differently.
Dogen, as you know, lived in the 13th century.
We've heard a lot of biographical information about him, so this is just a tidbit offering.
We have a wide range of Dogen literacy in our group.
We have people who have been reading with Chris for years, once a week, reading Dogen.
We have people who have done big studies, and we have people who aren't sure who Dogen is and why we would study him anyway.
So it's for all of us.
I steered clear of Dogen for a number of years.
Can everybody hear me okay?
I thought it was really difficult to understand.
I also had a teacher who preferred for us to primarily sit, and any information that I received about Dogen came from his Dharma talks.
He was a Dogen scholar, so there you go: we got Dogen, but we never read Dogen.
Some of the stuff that bowled me over for a long time was things like, in the Fukanzazengi that we chant, "think of not thinking."
How do you think of not thinking?
And the answer to that is non-thinking.
If you're coming up on this as an early practitioner, or even as just a person who hasn't read a lot of Dogen, it just doesn't seem to make that much sense.
But repetition is the key to our practice, and so we repeat and we reread.
I think that reading out loud is sometimes extremely helpful.
It's said that Huineng, the sixth ancestor, heard a person walking along chanting the Diamond Sutra, and that was what got him up and to the monastery.
In a more recent story, there's a woman named Wendy Johnson, who was one of the early practitioners at Tassajara.
She and her husband were tagged to start the garden effort at Green Gulch, so they were going to have to move from Tassajara to Green Gulch.
When they were young, they decided that they would walk there.
She relates in her book, Gardening at the Dragon's Gate, that she chanted the Mountains and Rivers Sutra as they went.
Anybody who's been in that country, just picture yourself walking through that Ventura Wilderness area.
I don't know how they did it once they got down to Highway One; they must have had to do something.
But anyway, it's an interesting thought, chanting the sutra over and over again.
I think that it gets into our bones.
We can't say anything that isn't somewhat misleading about our lives in an easy-to-grasp, bumper-sticker fashion.
Dogen instead goes for absorption in the words and offers us the chance to feel it through the aura of the text.
We can't paraphrase Dogen, really, so please enjoy the paradox of that statement while I paraphrase Dogen and talk about him a little bit.
By the way, "sutra" is used here deliberately.
Normally it means the direct words of the Buddha.
Dogen wants us to receive the mountains and waters as a direct experience and expression of the Buddha nature of mountains and waters, or rivers.
He wrote this fascicle, The Mountains and Rivers Sutra, evidently a week after he wrote his famous piece called Uji.
So time was on his mind.
Something that I learned from studying with Kathy Fisher is that often Dogen is not writing original material.
He is taking inspiration from older texts, and it's his poetic powers that make his writing so unique.
So it is for mountains and rivers.
While walking in the mountains, Su Tung Po, a Sung dynasty poet who lived from 1036 to 1101, wrote this:
*The sounds of the valley stream are his long broad tongue.
The forms of the mountain are his pure body.
In the night, I heard the myriad sutras uttered.
How can I relate what they mean?*
That's the poem that, it is said, inspired Dogen to write this sutra.
Well, might as well read a little.
I'm just going to read the first verse.
*Mountains and waters right now are the actualization of the ancient Buddha way.
Each abiding in its phenomenal expression realizes completeness.
Because mountains and waters have been active since before the empty eon, they are alive at this moment.
Because they have been the self since before form arose, they are emancipation realization.*
There are some multi-syllabic words in there.
I think what he's saying is we are who we are, and the mountains and waters are us.
They include us, we include them, and they are alive in this moment.
*Because mountains are high and broad, the way of riding the clouds is always reached in the mountains.
The inconceivable power of soaring in the wind comes freely from the mountains.*
How many of you have been up high in the mountains?
You know what that feels like.
I don't think I can ever forget one night, five days in on the trail, being in a place where I could really feel that not very many people had been there before.
It was so palpable, so strong.
Mountains have always been a place that has been used as a spiritual symbol.
We, of course, think about the monks who were visited, the old men in the hut way up in the mountains.
I think they've come to take an important spot in our reverence, maybe, for the natural world.
Of course, we live under a mountain, and under mountains, and next to waters.
So I love that.
*Because mountains are high and broad, the way of riding the clouds is always reached in the mountains.
The inconceivable power of soaring in the wind comes freely from the mountains.*
Some people say that the phrase, sorry, Mary, your glasses are not exactly what my eyes are.
*The way of riding the clouds is always reached in the mountains.
The inconceivable power of soaring in the wind comes freely from the mountains.*
That this is what happens, or that this is what we're invited into in meditation.
*The green mountains are always walking.
A stone woman gives birth to a child at night.*
This is not the first time we've come up with a stone woman.
There's another chant that we do: when the wooden man begins to sing, the stone woman gets up to dance.
Now, I find these things to be just amazing little images.
They're big images.
Why are they there?
I think it's to blast us out of what we think we know.
How does a stone woman get up to dance?
How does a stone woman give birth to a child at night?
I know that there's a sort of coded meaning of that as well as it being impossible.
I just kind of like thinking about that stone woman.
Who is she?
I think when we're in the mountains, we maybe come closest to this.
They talk about eons.
*Because they have been the self since before form arose.*
That's one.
Sorry, I missed one.
*Because mountains and waters have been active since before the empty eon, they are alive in this moment.*
It's kind of like, what is a kalpa?
There's a definition of what a kalpa is.
Basically, it's a long, long time, and the empty eon is the same way.
I think that Dogen is trying to help us pull the immense enormity of science into our spiritual essence, when the observer and the observed are the same thing.
Is there a physicist in the group?
Particle physics talks about this too.
I'm not one; I'm just going to trust that he was on to something a long time ago.
*Examine walking backward and backward walking.
And investigate the fact that walking forward and backward has never stopped since the very moment before form arose.
Since the time of the king of the empty eon.*
He's inviting us to, as we've heard before, take the backward step into unity, into beyond you and me.
We had some good breakout groups a couple of months ago about taking the backward step.
I'm looking at Paula, and I remember Paula and Arianne and I were talking about that together.
That reminds me of something that my husband always asks me: how come you Buddhists talk about the same stuff over and over all the time?
There's a lot to think about, there's a lot to remember.
I think that, once again, repetition brings us a little closer to something.
*Speaking of mind and speaking of essence is not agreeable to Buddha ancestors.
Confined words and phrases do not lead to liberation.*
It's about being fully engaged with your life in the present, the kind of experience that cannot be explained.
You could call it radical immediacy.
That's a Norman Fischer idea.
But really, it's all asking us to just live, to live actively.
The study is great, but we've got to jump in and live.
*Up into the mountains, down into the waters.*
In other words, all that he's saying about mountains, walking, flowing, and everything having no separation and no ending and no beginning, and their ongoingness, is available to us every minute.
If we can fully enter it, it's an act of living.
For some reason, I did not write the quote during the Tang dynasty, which is back in the 700s in China.
Oh, now I have the guy, the Chinese master, Qingyuan Weixin, who wrote:
*Before I had studied Chan for 30 years, I saw mountains as mountains and rivers as rivers.
When I arrived at a more intimate knowledge, I came to the point where I saw that the mountains are not mountains and the rivers are not rivers.
Now that I've got its very substance, I am at rest.
For it's just that I see mountains once again as mountains and rivers once again as rivers.*
If there's anybody here who's old enough to sing this with me, remember Donovan?
*First there is a mountain, then there is no mountain, then there is.
First there is a mountain, then there is no mountain, then there is.*
I think we saw this same kind of working in the Diamond Sutra, where the idea of the dialectic is brought in, where something is something, but then it's not something, and then it's something again.
I don't have a judgment on that, I don't have a real opinion on it, but it certainly comes up in Buddhist writing, and I think we're well served if we become familiar with the fact that it's there.
There's also a section on water that comes in to weave in.
I'm not going to talk about the whole Mountains and Rivers Sutra, because how could I?
Books have been written about it.
There are long study sessions.
But in the same way that mountains are considered a sort of spiritual place, water has been found to be incredibly powerful to our well-being.
There is an expression for finding peace in water, and it's called blue mind.
Has anyone heard of that?
Being on or near water has a stress-relieving and creativity-boosting impact on the brain.
Wallace J.
Nichols is the person I found this material from, and he wrote a book called Blue Mind.

He describes that phenomenon as a mildly meditative state that's inspired by water and takes advantage of the neurological connections formed over millennia that are still being discovered in newer technology like EEGs and MRIs.
I love that the neurological connections formed over millennia were reaching way down into something.
I personally really find this when I look at water.
I can be in a state and decide to [unclear: "take chukka nut instead of blue way"], so I can just look at water.
So try it.
It's about the present moment.
It's about animate and inanimate objects, because Dogen's telling us that the mountains and the waters are us, and we are the mountains and the waters.
I always think of Gary Snyder when I think of mountains and rivers, because he wrote an epic poem called Mountains and Rivers Without End.
I can't possibly reproduce the essence of that epic poem, but he is an important person in my Zen history, and so I'm going to share a poem that he read the last time I saw him in person.
It's called "Atomic Dawn."
*The day I first climbed Mount St.
Helens was August 13th, 1945.
Spirit Lake was far from the cities of the valley, and news came slow.
Though the first atomic bomb was dropped on Hiroshima August 6th, and the second dropped on Nagasaki August 9th, photographs didn't appear in the Portland Oregonian until August 12th.
Those papers must have been driven in to Spirit Lake on the 13th.
Early the morning of the 14th, I walked over to the lodge to check the bulletin board.
There were whole pages of the paper pinned up, photos of a blasted city from the air, the estimate of 150,000 dead in Hiroshima alone.
The American scientist quoted as saying, nothing will grow there again for 70 years.*
*The mountain sun on my shoulders, the fir forest smell, and the big tree shadows, feet in thin moccasins feeling the ground, and my heart still one with the snowpeak mountain at my back.
Horrified, blaming scientists and politicians and the government of the world, I swore a vow to myself, something like, by the purity and beauty and permanence of Mount St.
Helens, I will fight against this cruel, destructive power and those who would seek to use it for all my life.*
Well, he did the latter.
He did fight against warfare.
But as we all know, Mount St.
Helens was anything but permanent in its form anyway.
And as he said in his most recent visit to Hiroshima, there was a thriving and rebuilding culture that was alive.
So mountains move, water courses, the soil created from the minerals in mountains mixed with water, and they create something like this.
At the risk of sounding trite, it's all connected, and so are we.
So the question then is, right here and right now, how do I honor life?
How can I be in this present moment honoring life?
How can I take the opportunity and be here right now?
How do I deal with impermanence in my life?
How do I deal with this present moment?
Let our practice be our guide.
